messages.subject: New version of AHMbook R package
messages.subject_clean: New version of AHMbook R package
messages.body_plain:
We have wrapped up a new version of the AHMbook package, v. 0.1.1. Details of changes are below.

The new version depends on other packages, which you can install or update with

install.packages(c("unmarked", "plotrix", "sp", "raster", "RandomFields", "coda"))

If you have all those installed and you are running R 3.3.x, you can install the new package with

install.packages("AHMbook", repos = "http://mikemeredith.net/R")

The same URL <http://mikemeredith.net/R/> will get you to a page where you can download the source or binaries for manual installation.

New in version 0.1.1
Full help pages for all functions.
New names: plot.Nmix.resi -> plot_Nmix_resi and image.scale -> image_scale, to prevent clashes with R's 'plot' and 'image' generic functions.
Fewer dependencies, and all checked when you load AHMbook: no more "there is no package called xxx" when you try to run a function.
Changes to the "histograms" of counts, using transparent colours when two counts are plotted together.
The dragonfly data have been tidied up; do data(dragonfly) before use.
New functions for AHM Volume 2: simDynocc and simDCM.
The 'jay' dataset has migrated to 'unmarked' package.
Fixed: bugs involving 'logit'.
Fixed: data.fn() now corresponds to the code in section 4.3.
Fixed: simHDSg("point", ...), sim.spatialDS() and sim.spatialHDS() now work.
Fixed: plotting functions now restore the settings of the graphics window on exit.
Note: simComm("counts",...), simHDStr("point",...), and simHDSopen("point",...) give slightly different results even with the same seed; all the other simulations give the same values as before when set.seed() is used.
Thanks to Marc for help with the documentation and to Andy for finding some missing code.

messages.subject: Question on modeling richness in a two-step analysis
messages.subject_clean: Question on modeling richness in a two-step analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

 We are interested in exploring the effects of some covariates on a bird community using hierarchical community models with DA, with covariates. In addition, we want to explore how species richness is affected by some covariates. We suspect some covariates affecting occupancy could also affect species richness.

 I was looking at section 11.6.4 in AHM book (Modeling species richness in a two-step analysis) and I wonder if it would be right using this kind of model. The example in the book for this analysis uses posteriors from occupancy model 5 which does not include covariates. So the question is, it is right to use the same covariates in the occupancy model (first step) to model richness (second step)?, or the 2 step approach only works when occupancy is not affected by any covariates (or only different ones as in richness)?

 My guess is that it would not be correct to use the same covariates used to model occupancy to model richness, then in that case can only make inferences on richness computed from the occupancy models (discarding the use of two step analysis).

 Thoughts?

 Thank you!

 Andrea

 PS: Is there any new references using this approach?

-----

Andrea Paula Goijman, Ph.D

Grupo Ecología, Biodiversidad y Gestión Ambiental en Agroecosistemas Instituto de Recursos Biológicos CIRN - INTA Castelar, Argentina

Nicolas Repetto y de los Reseros s/n 1686 Hurlingham,

messages.subject: RE: Question on modeling richness in a two-step analysis
messages.subject_clean: Question on modeling richness in a two-step analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear Andrea,

I share your concerns about using the same covariates twice in such a two-step analysis. I think the best would be run two analyses, one for identifying covariates on occupancy and the other without covariates to get estimates of N for use in 2nd-stage modeling as in our book.

However, the very best would probably be to use a reparameterization of the community model due to Chris Sutherland and S. Tenan (see their 2-3 papers in MEE (I believe) recently) who develop a variant of the model where species richness IS a parameter and so can directly be modelled.

Best wishes  --  Marc

Hi Andrea,

Indeed this was the motivation of our (w/Simone Tenan) recent extensions of the community model:

1.       A multi-region community model for inference about geographic variation in species richness <https://www.researchgate.net/publication/292948994_A_multi-region_community_model_for_inference_about_geographic_variation_in_species_richness>

2.       Quantifying spatial variation in the size and structure of ecologically stratified communities <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12719/abstract>

We developed both using an application to an avian community.

Hopefully this is of use – which is the point ;) Please let me or Simone know if you have any questions!

Chris & Simone

Dear Andrea,

I share your concerns about using the same covariates twice in such a two-step analysis. I think the best would be run two analyses, one for identifying covariates on occupancy and the other without covariates to get estimates of N for use in 2nd-stage modeling as in our book.

However, the very best would probably be to use a reparameterization of the community model due to Chris Sutherland and S. Tenan (see their 2-3 papers in MEE (I believe) recently) who develop a variant of the model where species richness IS a parameter and so can directly be modelled.

Best wishes  --  Marc

Dear all,

 We are interested in exploring the effects of some covariates on a bird community using hierarchical community models with DA, with covariates. In addition, we want to explore how species richness is affected by some covariates. We suspect some covariates affecting occupancy could also affect species richness.

 I was looking at section 11.6.4 in AHM book (Modeling species richness in a two-step analysis) and I wonder if it would be right using this kind of model. The example in the book for this analysis uses posteriors from occupancy model 5 which does not include covariates. So the question is, it is right to use the same covariates in the occupancy model (first step) to model richness (second step)?, or the 2 step approach only works when occupancy is not affected by any covariates (or only different ones as in richness)?

 My guess is that it would not be correct to use the same covariates used to model occupancy to model richness, then in that case can only make inferences on richness computed from the occupancy models (discarding the use of two step analysis).

 Thoughts?

 Thank you!

 Andrea

 PS: Is there any new references using this approach?

messages.subject: Bayesian approach systematically overestimates sigma (SD)
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am quite stunned: I did some test on generated data, in the same way as
Marc & Andy recommend in their books, and found out that model estimates
from JAGS of the standard deviation of input data are systematically
overestimated by certain and fixed constant 1.20247, for N = 9!

The model is very simple:

model {

intcept ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
sigma ~ dunif(0, 10)

for (i in 1:N) {
    Y_exp[i] <- intcept
    Y[i] ~ dnorm(Y_exp[i], 1/sigma^2)
}

}

Now if we plot sigma against sd(Y), you will see the difference:

http://stats.stackexchange.com/q/257167/5509
(see the plot at this link)

The sigma estimated from the JAGS model is always greater by 1.20247!! Not
only in this simple model, but also the residual sigma
in linear regression is overestimated by approx the same constant (I tested
this in a different test). And since sd(Y) is the best unbiased predictor of
the distribution SD, the bayesian approach seriously overestimates the
parameter!

I tried to change the prior for sigma (or variance) to:

- sigma ~ dunif(0, 5) - no change
- half cauchy prior (from Gelman, pg 529) - no change
- dgamma prior - the slope is smaller, but it is still a difference!

It is possible that the slope will change with N. I only tested with N = 9.

I haven't tested WinBUGS/OpenBUGS or other MCMC tools, I guess the result
would be the same, since this is probably some statistical artifact (??)

The full code to reproduce this issue can be found here

http://artax.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/~ttel5535/pub/so/bayes_overestimates_sd-code.zip

Any thoughts why is this happening are very welcome!

Marc, did you observe this behaviour in your simulations?

Regards,

	Tomas

PS: You can also answer directly to the statistical forum here: http://stats.stackexchange.com/q/257167/5509

--

messages.body_plain:
Tomas,

I just replied to the forum thread, now copying that here as well.

I haven't checked everything in your zip file, but the problem seemed to be simple enough based on the JAGS model you have posted. The discrepancy between sd and JAGS output is due to sensitivity to the prior. To test this, you can use data cloning which relies on the same MCMC machinery to get MLE. If posterior mean is different from MLE, it is most likely due to the prior. You shouldn't expect MLE for N=9. You might want to ponder if you really want a Bayesian answer if this discrepancy bothers you. See this gist for a reproducible example and some results: https://gist.github.com/psolymos/c3388f9a6355cbf586c7e60c4b9bc946

The main results are these based on 100 replications:

#  Post.intcept      Post.sigma      MLE.intcept       MLE.sigma       Data.intcept
# Min.   :0.2056   Min.   :0.5033   Min.   :0.2071   Min.   :0.3940   Min.   :0.2069
# 1st Qu.:0.7295   1st Qu.:0.9569   1st Qu.:0.7311   1st Qu.:0.7504   1st Qu.:0.7310
# Median :0.9612   Median :1.1910   Median :0.9694   Median :0.9364   Median :0.9695
# Mean   :0.9942   Mean   :1.1782   Mean   :0.9960   Mean   :0.9259   Mean   :0.9960
# 3rd Qu.:1.2649   3rd Qu.:1.3977   3rd Qu.:1.2649   3rd Qu.:1.1071   3rd Qu.:1.2652
# Max.   :1.7428   Max.   :1.8451   Max.   :1.7435   Max.   :1.4376   Max.   :1.7433
#   Data.sigma
# Min.   :0.4171
# 1st Qu.:0.7944
# Median :0.9912
# Mean   :0.9802
# 3rd Qu.:1.1717
# Max.   :1.5212

Post = Posterior mean from JAGS, MLE = maximum likelihood estimate based on MCMC and data cloning, Data = is summaries based on mean() and sd().

Cheers,

Peter
